focusAreas.title: Get Legally Ready
focusAreas.summary: Before we open our Palestine House, we need to make sure the basic legal and business setup is in place.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to make sure:

- our local entity is properly registered, if required
- our Palestine House bank account is ready
- we have the right insurance
- we have any local permits or licenses we need
- our Palestine House agreement is signed
- we understand the basic Palestine House brand rules

The exact legal requirements will be different in every country and city, so we should always check what applies locally.

Our goal is simple:

__Be properly set up, protected and ready to operate.__

Step 1. Register Our Local Entity

We first check whether we need to register a company, social enterprise, nonprofit or other local entity.

What we need will depend on the country and city where we operate.

### __We should:__

- check what type of entity is right for us
- complete the local registration
- keep a copy of the registration documents
- make sure we know who is legally responsible for the entity

### __Simple question__

__Are we legally registered to operate?__

Step 2. Open Our Bank Account

We open a bank account in the name of our local Palestine House entity.

We should avoid using personal bank accounts for Palestine House money.

### __We should:__

- choose a suitable bank
- open the account in the organization’s name
- decide who can access the account
- decide who can approve payments

Simple question

__Can we receive and pay money through an official Palestine House account?__

Step 3. Arrange Insurance

We check what insurance we need for our venue and activities.

This may include things such as:

- public liability
- property
- staff
- events
- equipment

The exact requirements will depend on local law and the type of venue we operate.

### __We should:__

- ask a local insurance provider what is required
- choose suitable cover
- keep the policy details in one place
- note the renewal date

### __Simple question__

__Are we protected if something goes wrong?__

Step 4. Get the Right Permits and Licenses

We check whether our city requires any permits or licenses before we open.

These may depend on what we do.

For example:

- operating a venue
- serving food
- playing music
- hosting events
- selling alcohol, if applicable
- signage
- fire and safety requirements

### __We should:__

- make a simple list of what applies to us
- apply early
- keep copies of all approvals
- track renewal dates

### __Simple question__

__Are we allowed to do everything we plan to do in our venue?__

Step 5. Sign Our Palestine House Agreement

Before we operate as Palestine House, we complete and sign the agreement with Community Support.

This makes the relationship clear.

It should cover the basics such as:

- our right to use the Palestine House name and brand
- our responsibilities as a local operator
- the role of Community Support
- the standards we agree to follow

### __Simple question__

__Is our relationship with Community Support clearly agreed?__

Step 6. Understand the Basic Brand Rules

We make sure the team understands the short Palestine House Brand Guide.

We do not need to memorize everything.

We simply need to know:

- how to use the Palestine House name
- how to use the logo
- how to present our local house
- what we should not change without approval
- when to ask Community Support for help

### __Simple question__

__Can we represent Palestine House correctly and consistently?__

Our Final Check

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these six questions:

- Are we legally registered if required?
- Do we have an official bank account?
- Do we have the insurance we need?
- Do we have the required permits and licenses?
- Have we signed our Palestine House agreement?
- Do we understand the basic brand rules?

If yes, we are legally ready to move forward.

__Keep it simple.__
__Check what is required locally.__
__Keep the important documents together.__
__Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Plan the Money
focusAreas.summary: Before we open our Palestine House, we need a simple plan for the money.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to know:

- how much it will cost to open
- how much it will cost to run each month
- where our income will come from
- how much cash we need saved before we open

Costs and income will look different in every city, so we should build a plan that fits our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__Know our numbers and open with enough cash to feel safe.__

## __Step 1. Estimate Our Opening Costs__

We work out what it will cost to get our Palestine House ready to open.

This does not need to be a complex financial model.

### We should:

- list every one-time cost needed to open, like venue setup, furniture and first supplies
- get real quotes instead of guessing
- add a small buffer for surprises
- write the total in one place

### Simple question

__Do we know how much it will cost to open?__

## __Step 2. Estimate Our Monthly Running Costs__

We work out what it will cost to keep our Palestine House running each month.

This includes things like rent, staff and utilities.

### We should:

- list our fixed monthly costs, like rent and salaries
- list our variable monthly costs, like supplies and marketing
- add them together for one simple monthly number
- review this list every few months

### Simple question

__Do we know how much it will cost to run each month?__

## __Step 3. Plan Where Our Income Will Come From__

We think through how our Palestine House will actually make money.

It helps to know this before we open, not after.

### We should:

- list every way we expect to earn money, like memberships, F&B and events
- estimate a realistic monthly amount for each one
- avoid relying on just one source of income
- update these numbers as we learn more

### Simple question

__Do we know where our income will come from?__

## __Step 4. Know How Much Cash We Need Before Opening__

We make sure we have enough cash saved before we open our doors.

Income often takes a few months to catch up with costs.

### We should:

- add up our opening costs and a few months of running costs
- confirm we have this amount saved or committed
- keep a small extra buffer for the unexpected
- avoid opening before this is in place

### Simple question

__Do we have enough cash saved before we open?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we know how much it will cost to open?
- Do we know how much it will cost to run each month?
- Do we know where our income will come from?
- Do we have enough cash saved before we open?

If yes, we are financially ready to move forward.

__Keep it simple.
Check what is required locally.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Find and Prepare the Space
focusAreas.summary: Once we are legally ready, we need to find a venue that will work well for our Palestine House.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to think about:

- the location
- the size
- the rent
- accessibility
- how many people it can hold for events
- whether it works for food and drink
- basic safety
- the atmosphere it creates

What matters most will differ depending on the city and the kind of house we are building, so we should always check what fits our own space.

Our goal is simple:

__Find a space that feels right and works for the house we want to run.__

## __Step 1. Choose the Right Location__

The location shapes who can reach us and how the house feels in the neighborhood.

This is one of the most important choices we will make.

### We should:

- think about who our visitors are and where they live
- check how easy it is to reach on foot, by transit or by car
- look at what is nearby, like shops, schools or other cultural spaces
- visit at different times of day before deciding

### Simple question

__Is our location easy for our community to reach?__

## __Step 2. Choose the Right Size__

The space needs to be big enough for our programs, but not so big we cannot fill it or afford it.

Bigger is not always better.

### We should:

- think about how many people we expect day to day
- think about our biggest planned event
- check if there is room to grow later
- avoid taking on more space than we need

### Simple question

__Is the size right for what we plan to do?__

## __Step 3. Understand the Rent__

We need to know exactly what we are paying, and whether we can afford it every month.

This should be clear and comfortable, not stressful.

### We should:

- confirm the monthly rent and what it includes
- ask about deposits, increases and contract length
- compare the rent to our budget
- get everything in writing

### Simple question

__Can we comfortably afford this rent each month?__

## __Step 4. Check Accessibility__

Everyone in our community should be able to reach and enjoy the space.

This matters for visitors, artists and our own team.

### We should:

- check for step-free entry and accessible bathrooms
- check if public transport is nearby
- think about parking, if relevant
- ask what small changes could make it more welcoming

### Simple question

__Can everyone in our community access the space easily?__

## __Step 5. Check Event Capacity__

We should know how many people the space can safely and comfortably hold for events.

This helps us plan programs that actually fit.

### We should:

- ask about the maximum capacity for our type of venue
- picture the space set up for a full event
- check if furniture can be moved or stored easily
- plan for both small and larger gatherings

### Simple question

__Do we know how many people our space can hold?__

## __Step 6. Check F&B Potential__

If we plan to serve food or drinks, the space needs to support that safely.

It does not need to be a full restaurant kitchen.

### We should:

- check if there is a kitchen or prep area, or room to add one
- check the water, power and ventilation
- ask what food service permits we would need
- think about storage for supplies

### Simple question

__Can our space support the food and drink we want to offer?__

## __Step 7. Check Basic Safety__

Before anything else, the space needs to be safe for our team and visitors.

This comes before atmosphere or design.

### We should:

- check fire exits and fire safety equipment
- check the condition of floors, stairs and electrics
- ask about any past safety issues
- confirm what safety upgrades are needed before opening

### Simple question

__Is the space safe for our team and visitors?__

## __Step 8. Consider the Atmosphere__

The space should feel like Palestine House the moment someone walks in.

Numbers matter, but so does the feeling.

### We should:

- picture how the space will feel once it is set up
- think about light, sound and layout
- imagine a visitor’s first impression
- trust our instinct, not just the numbers

### Simple question

__Does this space feel right for Palestine House?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these eight questions:

- Is our location easy for our community to reach?
- Is the size right for what we plan to do?
- Can we comfortably afford this rent each month?
- Can everyone in our community access the space easily?
- Do we know how many people our space can hold?
- Can our space support the food and drink we want to offer?
- Is the space safe for our team and visitors?
- Does this space feel right for Palestine House?

If yes, we are ready to move forward with this space.

__Keep it simple.
Check what is required locally.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Build a Small Team
focusAreas.summary: As we get ready to open, we need to think about who will run our Palestine House day to day.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. A Palestine House should stay lean.

We simply need to make sure we have:

- a House Lead
- someone for operations and admin
- someone for programming and community
- part-time front-of-house or F&B support, if needed

Some of these roles can be combined, especially in a smaller house, so we should build a team that fits what we actually need.

Our goal is simple:

__Have a small, capable team that can run the house well.__

## __Step 1. Appoint a House Lead__

The House Lead holds the big picture and makes sure everything comes together.

Every house needs one clear point person.

### We should:

- choose one person to hold overall responsibility
- make sure they understand our mission and standards
- give them the authority to make day-to-day decisions
- connect them directly with Community Support for support

### Simple question

__Do we have one person leading the house?__

## __Step 2. Appoint Operations & Admin Support__

Someone needs to keep the practical side of the house running smoothly.

This role can be combined with others in a smaller house.

### We should:

- assign someone to handle money, admin and daily logistics
- make sure they understand our basic financial routines
- give them access to the tools they need
- decide how they report to the House Lead

### Simple question

__Do we have someone handling operations and admin?__

## __Step 3. Appoint Programming & Community Support__

Someone needs to bring our cultural programs and community connections to life.

This is the heart of what makes each house come alive.

### We should:

- assign someone to plan and run events and programs
- make sure they understand our community and audience
- connect them with the wider Palestine House network
- give them a simple way to plan the calendar

### Simple question

__Do we have someone leading programming and community?__

## __Step 4. Add Front-of-House or F&B Support, If Needed__

If we welcome visitors or serve food and drinks, we likely need some part-time help.

This does not need to be a full-time role.

### We should:

- decide if we need front-of-house or F&B support
- consider combining this with another role if the house is small
- keep the schedule simple and part-time where possible
- make sure this person understands basic service standards

### Simple question

__Do we have enough support to welcome visitors well?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we have one person leading the house?
- Do we have someone handling operations and admin?
- Do we have someone leading programming and community?
- Do we have enough support to welcome visitors well?

If yes, we have the small team we need to run the house well.

__Keep it simple.
Check what is required locally.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Get Ready To Open
focusAreas.summary: Once the space, team and money are in place, we need a simple countdown to opening day.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. A Palestine House should stay lean.

We simply need to know:

- what to do 90 days before we open
- what to do 30 days before we open
- what to do during opening week
- what to do on opening day itself

The exact timeline may shift depending on local permits and logistics, so we should always check what applies to our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__Be fully ready and confident when we open our doors.__

## __Step 1. Plan the 90-Day Countdown__

Ninety days out is when we lock the big pieces into place so nothing is left to chance later.

This is our last big planning push before the details take over.

### We should:

- confirm the venue, team and budget are in place
- finalize permits, licenses and insurance
- start booking the opening event and key suppliers
- set a realistic opening date

### Simple question

__Do we have a clear plan for the 90 days before opening?__

## __Step 2. Plan the 30-Day Countdown__

Thirty days out is when the details come together and we start testing what we have built.

This is where the house starts to feel real.

### We should:

- confirm furniture, equipment and signage are ordered or installed
- test our financial and F&B routines
- finalize the opening event details
- start promoting the opening date

### Simple question

__Do we have a clear plan for the 30 days before opening?__

## __Step 3. Plan Opening Week__

Opening week is for final checks, training and making sure the team feels ready.

This is not the time for surprises.

### We should:

- do a full walkthrough of the venue
- train the team on daily routines and emergency procedures
- confirm everything on our Pre-Opening Venue Checklist is done
- send final reminders to guests and partners

### Simple question

__Is our team ready for opening week?__

## __Step 4. Plan Opening Day__

Opening day should feel exciting, not chaotic, because everything was already prepared.

Let the team enjoy this moment.

### We should:

- follow a simple opening day run sheet
- assign clear roles for the day
- welcome visitors warmly and confidently
- take a moment to celebrate with the team

### Simple question

__Do we have a clear run sheet for opening day?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we open our doors, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we have a clear plan for the 90 days before opening?
- Do we have a clear plan for the 30 days before opening?
- Is our team ready for opening week?
- Do we have a clear run sheet for opening day?

If yes, we are ready to open our doors.

__Keep it simple.
Check what is required locally.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Money
focusAreas.summary: Once we are open, we need a simple way to stay on top of our money.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. We need basic financial control, not corporate finance.

We simply need to make sure we:

- record money coming in
- record money going out
- pay suppliers
- track the bank balance
- compare income with expenses once a month

If anything is unclear, our Community Support team is there to help, so we never have to figure out complex financial systems on our own.

Our goal is simple:

__Always know where our money stands.__

## __Step 1. Record Money Coming In__

Every time money comes into our Palestine House, we write it down.

This does not need to be complicated bookkeeping.

### We should:

- record every payment we receive, big or small
- note where the money came from
- do this as it happens, not weeks later
- keep receipts or proof together

### Simple question

__Do we record every payment we receive?__

## __Step 2. Record Money Going Out__

Every time we spend money, we write it down too.

This keeps us honest with ourselves about where money goes.

### We should:

- record every payment we make
- note what it was for
- keep receipts and invoices together
- avoid paying for things with no record

### Simple question

__Do we record every payment we make?__

## __Step 3. Pay Suppliers__

We pay the people and businesses who support our house on time and fairly.

Trust with suppliers is easy to lose and hard to rebuild.

### We should:

- know who we owe and how much
- pay on the agreed date
- keep a simple record of what's been paid
- flag any payment we can't make on time

### Simple question

__Are we paying our suppliers on time?__

## __Step 4. Track the Bank Balance__

We should always know how much money is actually in our account.

This is the simplest way to avoid surprises.

### We should:

- check the bank balance regularly
- compare it to what our records say
- notice anything unusual quickly
- keep the person responsible informed

### Simple question

__Do we know our current bank balance?__

## __Step 5. Compare Income with Expenses Once a Month__

Once a month, we take a step back and see the full picture.

This is where we catch problems early.

### We should:

- add up all income for the month
- add up all expenses for the month
- see if we made more than we spent
- decide if anything needs to change next month

### Simple question

__Do we compare income and expenses every month?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we record every payment we receive?
- Do we record every payment we make?
- Are we paying our suppliers on time?
- Do we know our current bank balance?
- Do we compare income and expenses every month?

If yes, we have basic financial control in place.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Daily House Operations
focusAreas.summary: Running our Palestine House day to day comes down to a few simple routines.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. We focus on simple routines.

We simply need to:

- open the house
- close the house
- keep it clean
- deal with basic maintenance
- make sure the venue is safe
- prepare spaces for events

The exact routine may look different depending on our venue, so we should build the schedule that fits our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__A house that opens, runs and closes smoothly every day.__

## __Step 1. Open the House__

Every day starts with a simple routine that gets the house ready to welcome people.

A calm opening sets the tone for the whole day.

### We should:

- unlock and switch on what's needed
- do a quick walk-through before anyone arrives
- set up the spaces we'll use that day
- make sure the team knows the plan for the day

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple routine for opening each day?__

## __Step 2. Close the House__

Closing well protects the space and sets tomorrow up for an easy start.

This should not be rushed at the last minute.

### We should:

- lock up and switch off what's needed
- put spaces back in order
- check nothing was left unattended
- note anything that needs attention tomorrow

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple routine for closing each day?__

## __Step 3. Keep It Clean__

A clean house feels welcoming and shows we care about the space.

This is one of the easiest ways to make a good impression.

### We should:

- clean shared spaces every day
- deal with spills or mess right away
- assign who is responsible for what
- do a deeper clean on a regular schedule

### Simple question

__Is our house clean and cared for every day?__

## __Step 4. Deal with Basic Maintenance__

Small problems are easy to fix early and harder to ignore later.

A well-kept house feels safer and more welcoming.

### We should:

- check for anything broken or worn
- fix small issues quickly
- keep a simple list of repairs needed
- know who to call for bigger repairs

### Simple question

__Do we deal with maintenance issues quickly?__

## __Step 5. Make Sure the Venue Is Safe__

Safety comes before everything else we do in the house.

This protects our visitors, our team and our house.

### We should:

- check fire exits and safety equipment regularly
- keep walkways and exits clear
- know what to do in an emergency
- fix safety issues immediately, not later

### Simple question

__Is our venue safe for visitors and our team?__

## __Step 6. Prepare Spaces for Events__

Spaces often need to be reset or rearranged for different programs.

A well-prepared space lets the event, not the setup, take center stage.

### We should:

- know what each event needs from the space
- set up and reset spaces between uses
- check everything is ready before guests arrive
- return the space to its normal state afterward

### Simple question

__Are our spaces ready before every event?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we call the day done, we should be able to answer yes to these six questions:

- Do we have a simple routine for opening each day?
- Do we have a simple routine for closing each day?
- Is our house clean and cared for every day?
- Do we deal with maintenance issues quickly?
- Is our venue safe for visitors and our team?
- Are our spaces ready before every event?

If yes, our house runs smoothly every day.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.summary: If our Palestine House has a café or simple F&B offer, we keep it lean.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to:

- know what we sell
- know the cost
- track stock
- avoid waste
- keep the area clean
- reconcile daily sales

Food safety and hygiene rules will differ depending on our city, so we should always check what applies locally.

Our goal is simple:

__Run a simple, profitable F&B offer without extra complexity.__

## __Step 1. Know What We Sell__

We keep our menu simple and clear, so our team and our visitors always know what's on offer.

A short menu is easier to run well than a long one.

### We should:

- keep the menu short and easy to prepare
- write it down clearly, with prices
- update it whenever something changes
- make sure the team knows it by heart

### Simple question

__Do we have a clear, simple menu?__

## __Step 2. Know the Cost__

We should know exactly what each item costs us to make, so we know if we're actually making money.

A good menu can still lose money if the pricing is wrong.

### We should:

- work out the cost of ingredients for each item
- add in packaging, if we use it
- compare the cost to the selling price
- adjust prices if the margin is too thin

### Simple question

__Do we know the true cost of what we sell?__

## __Step 3. Track Stock__

Knowing what we have on hand helps us order the right amount and avoid running out.

This does not need a complex system.

### We should:

- keep a simple list of what's in stock
- check stock levels regularly
- order before we run low
- note what sells fast and what doesn't

### Simple question

__Do we know what stock we have at all times?__

## __Step 4. Avoid Waste__

Wasted food is wasted money, so we keep an eye on what doesn't get used.

Small habits here add up over time.

### We should:

- order based on what we actually sell
- use older stock before newer stock
- notice patterns in what gets thrown away
- adjust what we buy based on what we learn

### Simple question

__Are we keeping waste to a minimum?__

## __Step 5. Keep the Area Clean__

A clean F&B area is safe, welcoming and simply expected.

This protects our visitors and our reputation.

### We should:

- clean surfaces and equipment every day
- follow basic food safety practices
- keep cleaning supplies stocked and accessible
- do a deeper clean on a regular schedule

### Simple question

__Is our F&B area clean and safe?__

## __Step 6. Reconcile Daily Sales__

At the end of each day, we check that what we sold matches what we took in.

This catches mistakes early, before they add up.

### We should:

- count the cash and card sales at the end of the day
- compare it to what the till or record shows
- note any differences
- record the day's total simply and clearly

### Simple question

__Do we reconcile our sales every day?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we call it a good F&B setup, we should be able to answer yes to these six questions:

- Do we have a clear, simple menu?
- Do we know the true cost of what we sell?
- Do we know what stock we have at all times?
- Are we keeping waste to a minimum?
- Is our F&B area clean and safe?
- Do we reconcile our sales every day?

If yes, our F&B offer is simple, safe and under control.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Members and Visitors
focusAreas.summary: Our members and visitors are at the heart of our Palestine House, so we look after them well.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. We do not overcomplicate membership.

We simply need to:

- register members
- welcome them
- keep their contact details
- track renewals
- collect feedback

What feels right for membership may differ depending on our community, so we should build an approach that fits our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__Members and visitors who feel welcomed and stay connected.__

## __Step 1. Register Members__

When someone joins as a member, we capture the basics so we can stay in touch and keep good records.

This should take a minute, not a form full of questions.

### We should:

- use one simple sign-up form for everyone
- collect only the details we actually need
- confirm the membership type and any fee
- send a simple welcome message once registered

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple way to register members?__

## __Step 2. Welcome Them__

A warm welcome is often what makes someone want to come back.

First impressions matter more than paperwork.

### We should:

- greet new members and visitors personally
- explain what the house offers, briefly
- introduce them to the space and team
- make them feel like they belong from day one

### Simple question

__Do we welcome members and visitors well?__

## __Step 3. Keep Their Contact Details__

Good contact details let us stay connected and share what's happening at the house.

A simple list is enough, as long as it is accurate.

### We should:

- keep a simple, organized list of contacts
- keep the information up to date
- store it securely and respectfully
- use it only for Palestine House communication

### Simple question

__Do we keep our contact list accurate and organized?__

## __Step 4. Track Renewals__

We should know when memberships are coming up for renewal, so no one lapses by accident.

A quiet reminder goes a long way.

### We should:

- know when each membership is due to renew
- send a simple reminder ahead of time
- make renewing quick and easy
- follow up gently if someone doesn't renew

### Simple question

__Do we track membership renewals?__

## __Step 5. Collect Feedback__

Members and visitors can tell us what's working and what isn't, if we ask.

Small, honest feedback is more useful than a long survey.

### We should:

- ask for feedback regularly, not just once
- keep the questions short and simple
- actually read and discuss what we hear
- make small improvements based on what we learn

### Simple question

__Do we regularly collect feedback from members and visitors?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we have a simple way to register members?
- Do we welcome members and visitors well?
- Do we keep our contact list accurate and organized?
- Do we track membership renewals?
- Do we regularly collect feedback from members and visitors?

If yes, our members and visitors feel valued and connected.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Team
focusAreas.summary: Once we are open, we need a simple way to look after our small team.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. Small houses need simple people management.

We simply need to:

- schedule staff
- know who is responsible for what
- talk about performance regularly
- deal with problems quickly

What feels right may differ depending on our team size, so we should build an approach that fits our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__A small team that works well together and feels supported.__

## __Step 1. Schedule Staff__

A clear schedule means everyone knows when they're working and the house is always covered.

This should be simple to check and easy to update.

### We should:

- plan the schedule ahead of time
- share it with the whole team early
- cover busy times and events properly
- leave room for time off and sick days

### Simple question

__Do we have a clear staff schedule?__

## __Step 2. Know Who Is Responsible for What__

When everyone knows their role, less falls through the cracks.

This matters even more when the team is small.

### We should:

- make sure each person knows their main responsibilities
- avoid leaving tasks with no clear owner
- write down roles simply, if helpful
- revisit this as the team grows or changes

### Simple question

__Does everyone know what they're responsible for?__

## __Step 3. Talk About Performance Regularly__

Short, regular check-ins help people grow and catch small issues before they grow.

This does not need to feel formal.

### We should:

- check in with each team member regularly
- give honest, kind feedback
- recognize what's going well
- agree on what to improve together

### Simple question

__Do we check in on performance regularly?__

## __Step 4. Deal with Problems Quickly__

Small problems are easier to solve than ones we've let sit for months.

Waiting rarely makes things easier.

### We should:

- address issues as soon as we notice them
- listen before deciding what to do
- be fair and consistent
- ask our Community Support team for help with anything difficult

### Simple question

__Do we deal with problems quickly and fairly?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we have a clear staff schedule?
- Does everyone know what they're responsible for?
- Do we check in on performance regularly?
- Do we deal with problems quickly and fairly?

If yes, our team is well managed and supported.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Monthly Check-Up
focusAreas.summary: Instead of complex performance management, we have one monthly "How are we doing?" review.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply look at:

- visitors
- members
- events
- income
- expenses
- problems
- next month's priorities

What matters most may differ depending on our house and community, so we should focus on what's most useful for us.

Our goal is simple:

__Know how we are doing, and what to focus on next.__

## __Step 1. Look at Visitors__

We check how many people came through our doors and what that tells us.

A simple count is enough to spot a trend.

### We should:

- count visitors for the month
- compare it to previous months
- notice any patterns, like busy days or events
- think about what brought people in

### Simple question

__Do we know how many visitors we had this month?__

## __Step 2. Look at Members__

We check how our membership is growing, or where it needs attention.

Small changes are easier to catch monthly than yearly.

### We should:

- count new members and any who left
- check how many renewals came through
- notice if any group needs more attention
- celebrate any growth, even small

### Simple question

__Do we know where our membership stands?__

## __Step 3. Look at Events__

We look back at what we ran and how it went.

This helps us plan better next time.

### We should:

- list the events we held this month
- note attendance and feedback
- see what worked and what didn't
- think about what to repeat or change

### Simple question

__Do we know how our events performed this month?__

## __Step 4. Look at Income__

We check what actually came in, not just what we expected.

Real numbers matter more than the plan.

### We should:

- add up income from all sources
- compare it to our budget
- notice which income grew or dropped
- understand why, if something changed

### Simple question

__Do we know what we earned this month?__

## __Step 5. Look at Expenses__

We check what we spent, and whether it matched our plan.

This is where we catch costs creeping up.

### We should:

- add up expenses for the month
- compare it to our budget
- notice anything unusually high or low
- flag anything that needs attention

### Simple question

__Do we know what we spent this month?__

## __Step 6. Look at Problems__

We name what went wrong, honestly and without blame.

Naming a problem is the first step to fixing it.

### We should:

- list any problems that came up
- talk about them openly as a team
- decide what caused them
- agree on how to prevent them next time

### Simple question

__Have we honestly looked at what went wrong?__

## __Step 7. Set Next Month's Priorities__

We use what we learned to decide what matters most next month.

A short, clear list beats a long, vague one.

### We should:

- pick a few clear priorities, not a long list
- make sure the whole team knows them
- connect priorities to what we just reviewed
- ask our Community Support team for help if needed

### Simple question

__Do we have clear priorities for next month?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we close the month out, we should be able to answer yes to these seven questions:

- Do we know how many visitors we had this month?
- Do we know where our membership stands?
- Do we know how our events performed this month?
- Do we know what we earned this month?
- Do we know what we spent this month?
- Have we honestly looked at what went wrong?
- Do we have clear priorities for next month?

If yes, we have a clear picture of how we're doing.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Plan the Calendar
focusAreas.summary: Before we plan any single event, we start with the calendar as a whole — a simple picture of what is coming up.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. We think only about the basics.

We simply need to know:

- what we're doing
- who it's for
- when it happens
- who's involved
- how much it will cost

What fits our calendar will differ depending on our community and season, so we should build a calendar that fits our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__A clear, simple calendar everyone can follow.__

## __Step 1. Decide What We're Doing__

Every event or program starts with a clear idea of what it actually is.

Keep the idea simple enough to explain in one sentence.

### We should:

- describe the event or program in one simple sentence
- keep the idea focused, not trying to do too much at once
- make sure it fits our mission and space
- write it down so everyone understands it the same way

### Simple question

__Do we know what we're planning?__

## __Step 2. Know Who It's For__

A clear picture of our audience helps us plan something that actually connects.

Not every event is for everyone, and that is fine.

### We should:

- think about who we want to reach
- consider what they'd enjoy or need
- keep our community in mind, not just numbers
- adjust the idea if it doesn't fit our audience

### Simple question

__Do we know who this is for?__

## __Step 3. Set When It Happens__

A clear date and time on the calendar turns an idea into a real plan.

Vague timing is where good ideas stall.

### We should:

- pick a realistic date and time
- check it doesn't clash with other events
- give ourselves enough time to prepare
- add it to the shared calendar

### Simple question

__Do we have a clear date and time?__

## __Step 4. Know Who's Involved__

Every event needs people behind it, and everyone should know their part.

Unclear roles are one of the biggest causes of last-minute stress.

### We should:

- decide who's leading the event
- identify who else needs to help
- involve artists, speakers or partners if needed
- make sure everyone knows what they're responsible for

### Simple question

__Do we know who's involved and what they'll do?__

## __Step 5. Know How Much It Will Cost__

A simple cost estimate helps us plan realistically from the start.

This does not need to be exact, just honest.

### We should:

- estimate the main costs, like space, artists or supplies
- check it fits within our budget
- decide if the event needs to earn money or is purely community-focused
- ask our Community Support team for help if the budget feels unclear

### Simple question

__Do we know roughly what this will cost?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we know what we're planning?
- Do we know who this is for?
- Do we have a clear date and time?
- Do we know who's involved and what they'll do?
- Do we know roughly what this will cost?

If yes, we have a clear plan to move forward with.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Plan an Event
focusAreas.summary: Once we know what's on the calendar, we plan each event the same simple way, every time.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. Every event can use the same simple process.

We simply need to:

- use the same checklist for every event
- have a simple run sheet for the day
- keep a guest list
- set a simple budget
- collect feedback afterward

The scale of each event may differ, so we should adjust the details while keeping the process the same.

Our goal is simple:

__A repeatable process that makes every event easier to plan.__

## __Step 1. Use the Same Checklist Every Time__

A repeatable checklist means we never start from scratch, no matter the event.

The same process works whether the event is small or big.

### We should:

- use one simple checklist for every event
- go through it from planning to wrap-up
- update it if we learn something new
- keep it easy enough to use under time pressure

### Simple question

__Do we use the same checklist for every event?__

## __Step 2. Build a Simple Run Sheet__

A run sheet turns the plan into a clear timeline for the day.

This is what keeps the day calm, not chaotic.

### We should:

- list the day's activities in order, with times
- assign who's doing what
- share it with everyone involved
- keep a copy on hand during the event

### Simple question

__Do we have a run sheet for the day?__

## __Step 3. Keep a Guest List__

Knowing who's coming helps us prepare properly and follow up afterward.

It also helps us make people feel personally welcomed.

### We should:

- keep a simple list of invited and confirmed guests
- note any special requirements
- use it to welcome people by name where possible
- keep it for future invitations

### Simple question

__Do we have a guest list for this event?__

## __Step 4. Set a Simple Budget__

A basic budget keeps spending under control and shows if the event makes sense financially.

This does not need to be complicated, just honest.

### We should:

- estimate the main costs before we commit
- track what we actually spend
- compare it to what we planned
- decide if the event needs to cover its costs

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple budget for this event?__

## __Step 5. Collect Feedback Afterward__

A quick check-in after the event helps us learn and improve next time.

This should take minutes, not a long survey.

### We should:

- ask a few simple questions after the event
- ask both guests and the team
- note what worked and what didn't
- carry what we learn into the next event

### Simple question

__Do we collect feedback after every event?__

## __Our Final Check__

Before we run the event, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we use the same checklist for every event?
- Do we have a run sheet for the day?
- Do we have a guest list for this event?
- Do we have a simple budget for this event?
- Do we collect feedback after every event?

If yes, we have a simple, repeatable way to plan events.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Work with Artists and Speakers
focusAreas.summary: When we bring in artists or speakers, we treat them professionally while keeping things simple.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This should be professional but easy.

We simply need to:

- agree on terms with a simple written agreement
- collect their basic information ahead of time
- take care of their hospitality needs
- pay them on time
- keep the paperwork light, not bureaucratic

What's customary for artists and speakers may differ by city, so we should check what fits our own community.

Our goal is simple:

__Artists and speakers who feel respected and well looked after.__

# __Step 1. Agree on Terms in Writing__

A simple written agreement protects both sides and avoids misunderstandings later.

This does not need to be a long legal document.

### We should:

- use a simple artist or speaker agreement
- confirm the date, fee and what's expected
- put it in writing before the event
- keep a signed copy on file

### Simple question

__Do we have a written agreement in place?__

# __Step 2. Collect Their Information Ahead of Time__

A little information beforehand helps everything run smoothly on the day.

This avoids surprises for everyone.

### We should:

- use a simple information form
- ask about technical or space needs
- ask about any dietary or accessibility needs
- confirm arrival time and contact details

### Simple question

__Do we have their information before the event?__

# __Step 3. Take Care of Their Hospitality__

A little care and hospitality goes a long way in how welcomed someone feels.

This reflects who we are as a house.

### We should:

- prepare a simple welcome, like water or refreshments
- make sure someone greets them on arrival
- have a comfortable space for them to prepare
- check in with them during the event

### Simple question

__Are we ready to host them well?__

# __Step 4. Pay Them on Time__

Timely, fair payment is one of the most respectful things we can do.

This builds trust for future collaborations too.

### We should:

- agree on the payment amount and method in advance
- pay by the agreed date
- use a simple payment form or record
- follow up quickly if there's a delay

### Simple question

__Are we paying artists and speakers on time?__

# __Step 5. Keep the Paperwork Light__

The process should feel professional, not bureaucratic.

Simplicity makes it easier for artists and speakers to say yes.

### We should:

- use the same simple templates every time
- avoid unnecessary steps or approvals
- keep everything in one place
- ask our Community Support team if something feels too complicated

### Simple question

__Is our process simple, not bureaucratic?__

# __Our Final Check__

Before we confirm an artist or speaker, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we have a written agreement in place?
- Do we have their information before the event?
- Are we ready to host them well?
- Are we paying artists and speakers on time?
- Is our process simple, not bureaucratic?

If yes, we work with artists and speakers professionally and simply.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.summary: Once an event is planned, we let people know about it the same simple way every time.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. The house should not need to create a marketing system every time.

We simply need to:

- follow the same simple marketing checklist
- use ready-made templates for social media posts
- send a simple email invitation
- share it with our community and partners
- track roughly how many people we reached

What works best may differ depending on our community and the platforms people actually use, so we should adjust the channels while keeping the process simple.

Our goal is simple:

__The right people hear about our events, without extra work each time.__

# __Step 1. Follow the Same Simple Marketing Checklist__

A repeatable checklist means we don't have to figure out promotion from scratch every time.

The same steps work for a small gathering or a big launch.

### We should:

- use one simple checklist for every event
- start promoting with enough lead time
- go through it step by step
- update it if we learn something that works better

### Simple question

__Do we use the same checklist to promote every event?__

# __Step 2. Use Ready-Made Social Media Templates__

Ready templates make it quick to post consistently, without starting from a blank page.

This keeps our posts looking like Palestine House every time.

### We should:

- use our existing social media templates
- fill in the event details clearly
- post on the platforms our community actually uses
- keep the look and voice consistent with Palestine House

### Simple question

__Do we use ready-made templates for social posts?__

# __Step 3. Send a Simple Email Invitation__

A clear email reaches people directly and gives them everything they need to attend.

This works even for people who aren't on social media.

### We should:

- use our simple email invitation template
- include the what, when, where and how to join
- send it with enough notice
- send a short reminder closer to the date

### Simple question

__Do we send a simple email invitation?__

# __Step 4. Share It with Our Community and Partners__

Our community and partners can help spread the word further than we can alone.

Word of mouth is often our strongest channel.

### We should:

- share the event with our members and regular visitors
- ask partners to help pass it along
- make it easy for people to share themselves
- personally invite anyone we especially want there

### Simple question

__Do we share the event with our community and partners?__

# __Step 5. Track Roughly How Many People We Reached__

A rough sense of our reach helps us understand what's working, without needing complex tools.

This does not need to be exact.

### We should:

- note how many people saw or responded to our posts
- note how many opened or replied to the email
- compare it loosely to past events
- carry what we learn into the next promotion

### Simple question

__Do we have a rough sense of how many people we reached?__

# __Our Final Check__

Before the event, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we use the same checklist to promote every event?
- Do we use ready-made templates for social posts?
- Do we send a simple email invitation?
- Do we share the event with our community and partners?
- Do we have a rough sense of how many people we reached?

If yes, the right people know about our event.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Learn the Event
focusAreas.summary: After every event, we take a few minutes to look back and learn.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. No long reports.

We simply need to ask:

- how many people came
- whether people enjoyed it
- whether we made or lost money
- what to repeat or change

What matters most may differ from event to event, so we should focus on what is most useful each time.

Our goal is simple:

__A quick, honest look back that helps the next event be even better.__

__Step 1. Count How Many Came__

A simple headcount tells us whether the event reached the people we hoped for.

This does not need to be exact, just close enough to be useful.

### We should:

- count or estimate attendance
- compare it to what we expected
- note if certain groups showed up more or less than planned
- keep the number simple and easy to record

### Simple question

__Do we know how many people came?__

__Step 2. Ask If People Enjoyed It__

A quick sense of how people felt tells us more than numbers alone.

This can be a few conversations, not a survey.

### We should:

- ask a few guests directly how it went
- notice the mood and energy during the event
- collect a couple of quick comments if possible
- listen for what people mention most

### Simple question

__Do we know if people enjoyed it?__

__Step 3. Check If We Made or Lost Money__

A simple look at income against costs tells us if the event made sense financially.

Not every event needs to earn money, but we should still know.

### We should:

- add up what the event brought in
- add up what it cost to run
- see if we made, broke even, or lost money
- note this for future planning

### Simple question

__Do we know if we made or lost money?__

__Step 4. Decide What to Repeat or Change__

Every event teaches us something we can use next time.

This is where the real improvement happens.

### We should:

- note what worked well
- note what we'd do differently
- decide what to repeat as-is
- share what we learned with the team

### Simple question

__Do we know what to repeat or change next time?__

__Our Final Check__

After the event, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we know how many people came?
- Do we know if people enjoyed it?
- Do we know if we made or lost money?
- Do we know what to repeat or change next time?

If yes, we've learned what we need from this event.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.summary: We don't have to do everything alone.
focusAreas.guideMd:
When it's useful, we can draw on the wider Palestine House network and Aswātna.

This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to know how to:

- ask for programming support when useful
- request artists from the network
- collaborate with other houses
- take part in shared network programs

What is available may differ depending on timing and location, so we should check what is possible for our own house.

Our goal is simple:

__Access to a wider network, used only when it genuinely helps us.__

__Step 1. Ask for Programming Support When Useful__

If we need help with a program or event, we don't have to figure it out alone.

Support is there when it genuinely helps.

### We should:

- know what kind of support is available
- use a simple request form when we need help
- be clear about what we're asking for
- reach out to our Community Support team early, not at the last minute

### Simple question

__Do we know how to ask for programming support?__

__Step 2. Request Artists from the Network__

Sometimes the right artist for our program is already connected to another house or Aswātna.

This can open doors we would not have on our own.

### We should:

- check if an artist we want is already part of the network
- use a simple request form to ask
- give enough notice for scheduling
- confirm details directly with the artist once connected

### Simple question

__Do we know how to request an artist from the network?__

__Step 3. Collaborate with Other Houses__

Working with another Palestine House can bring in new ideas, audiences and support.

We are part of something bigger than one house.

### We should:

- reach out directly to another house when it makes sense
- use a simple collaboration request
- agree on roles and costs upfront
- keep the process light and friendly

### Simple question

__Do we know how to collaborate with another house?__

__Step 4. Take Part in Shared Network Programs__

Some programs are designed to run across many houses at once, and we can join in.

This lets us offer more without building everything ourselves.

### We should:

- know what shared programs are happening
- use a simple form to confirm our participation
- adapt the program to fit our own house
- share how it went afterward

### Simple question

__Do we know how to take part in shared network programs?__

__Our Final Check__

Before we reach out to the network, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we know how to ask for programming support?
- Do we know how to request an artist from the network?
- Do we know how to collaborate with another house?
- Do we know how to take part in shared network programs?

If yes, we know how to connect with the wider network when it helps us.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Marketing
focusAreas.summary: We need basic help to make people aware of our house and its programs.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to:

- plan marketing activities month by month
- keep a simple content calendar
- send a newsletter
- reach out to press when it's worth it
- get good photos of our house and events

What works best may differ by city and community, so we should focus on the channels that reach our own audience.

Our goal is simple:

__More people know about our house and want to be part of it.__

__Step 1. Plan Marketing Activities Month by Month__

A simple monthly plan means we're not scrambling to promote things at the last minute.

This does not need to be a full strategy document.

### We should:

- list what needs promoting each month
- match marketing effort to what's actually happening
- plan a little ahead, not just react
- keep the plan realistic for our size

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple marketing plan for the month?__

__Step 2. Keep a Simple Content Calendar__

A content calendar helps us post consistently, without deciding what to share every single day.

A little planning saves a lot of last-minute stress.

### We should:

- plan our posts a few weeks ahead
- mix event promotion with everyday house content
- keep it flexible enough to add things last minute
- avoid leaving long gaps with no posts

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple content calendar?__

__Step 3. Send a Newsletter__

A newsletter keeps our community updated without them having to check social media constantly.

Consistency matters more than length.

### We should:

- use a simple, consistent newsletter template
- send it on a regular schedule
- keep the content short and useful
- make it easy for people to sign up

### Simple question

__Do we send a regular newsletter?__

__Step 4. Reach Out to Press When It's Worth It__

Not every event needs press coverage, but the right moment can bring real attention.

This works best when we are selective.

### We should:

- decide which events are worth press attention
- use a simple press release template
- reach out to relevant local media
- follow up politely if we don't hear back

### Simple question

__Do we reach out to press when it makes sense?__

__Step 5. Get Good Photos of Our House and Events__

Good photos make everything else we share look more welcoming and real.

This is one of the simplest ways to improve our marketing.

### We should:

- take photos regularly, not just at big events
- use a simple photography brief so shots are consistent
- ask permission before photographing people
- keep photos organized and easy to find

### Simple question

__Do we have good photos to use?__

__Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we have a simple marketing plan for the month?
- Do we have a simple content calendar?
- Do we send a regular newsletter?
- Do we reach out to press when it makes sense?
- Do we have good photos to use?

If yes, people know about our house and what we offer.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.summary: Sponsorship and fundraising help us grow, and we keep the process simple enough for a small team to run.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. Make this easy enough for a small team to use.

We simply need to:

- put together a simple sponsorship proposal
- keep a list of potential sponsors
- use a simple partnership agreement
- track grant opportunities
- apply for grants with a simple template

What is available may differ by city and community, so we should focus on the sponsors and grants that make sense for us.

Our goal is simple:

__Extra support that helps us grow, without overwhelming our small team.__

__Step 1. Put Together a Simple Sponsorship Proposal__

A clear, simple proposal makes it easy for a sponsor to say yes.

This does not need to be a long pitch deck.

### We should:

- use our simple sponsorship proposal template
- explain what we offer and what we're asking for
- keep it short enough to read in a few minutes
- tailor it slightly for each sponsor

### Simple question

__Do we have a simple sponsorship proposal ready?__

__Step 2. Keep a List of Potential Sponsors__

A simple list helps us know who to approach and keep track of conversations.

This avoids losing track of good leads.

### We should:

- list businesses and organizations that fit our house
- note who we've contacted and when
- track what stage each conversation is at
- update the list as relationships grow

### Simple question

__Do we keep a list of potential sponsors?__

__Step 3. Use a Simple Partnership Agreement__

A short written agreement keeps expectations clear on both sides.

This protects the relationship, not just the paperwork.

### We should:

- use our simple partnership agreement template
- confirm what each side is offering
- agree on how long the partnership lasts
- keep a signed copy on file

### Simple question

__Do we use a simple partnership agreement?__

__Step 4. Track Grant Opportunities__

Knowing what grants exist and when they're due helps us apply on time.

Missed deadlines are missed opportunities.

### We should:

- keep a simple list of relevant grants
- note deadlines and requirements
- check the list regularly
- avoid missing opportunities because we forgot

### Simple question

__Do we track grant opportunities?__

__Step 5. Apply for Grants with a Simple Template__

A reusable template makes applying for grants faster and less stressful.

We do not need to reinvent the wheel each time.

### We should:

- use our simple grant application template
- adapt it to each grant's specific questions
- ask our Community Support team for help if needed
- keep copies of what we submit

### Simple question

__Do we use a simple template when applying for grants?__

__Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we have a simple sponsorship proposal ready?
- Do we keep a list of potential sponsors?
- Do we use a simple partnership agreement?
- Do we track grant opportunities?
- Do we use a simple template when applying for grants?

If yes, we have a simple way to grow support for our house.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.summary: Partnerships help us do more than we could alone, so we build simple, useful relationships with others in our city.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated.

We simply need to know how to work with:

- universities
- cultural groups
- businesses
- NGOs
- community organizations

Who's available and relevant will differ by city, so we should build the partnerships that make sense for our own community.

Our goal is simple:

__A small circle of partners who genuinely help us grow.__

__Step 1. Work with Universities__

Universities can bring students, researchers and academic energy to our programs.

A simple collaboration can go a long way.

### We should:

- identify departments or student groups that fit our mission
- offer something useful, like space, speakers or projects
- keep the relationship simple and mutually beneficial
- start with one small collaboration before something bigger

### Simple question

__Do we have a way to work with universities?__

__Step 2. Work with Cultural Groups__

Other cultural organizations often share our audience and our values.

We are stronger together than apart.

### We should:

- identify cultural groups active in our city
- look for ways to co-host or cross-promote
- respect each other's identity and mission
- build relationships before asking for anything big

### Simple question

__Do we have a way to work with cultural groups?__

__Step 3. Work with Businesses__

Local businesses can support us with sponsorship, space, supplies or expertise.

A clear, fair offer makes it easy for them to say yes.

### We should:

- identify businesses that fit our values
- offer something simple in return, like visibility
- use our simple partnership agreement
- keep the ask clear and specific

### Simple question

__Do we have a way to work with businesses?__

__Step 4. Work with NGOs__

Other NGOs can offer expertise, networks or shared programs that strengthen our work.

We are usually working toward similar goals.

### We should:

- identify NGOs working on similar issues
- look for ways to collaborate, not compete
- be clear about what each side brings
- keep the relationship simple and respectful

### Simple question

__Do we have a way to work with NGOs?__

__Step 5. Work with Community Organizations__

Community organizations often know our neighborhood and audience better than anyone.

They can be some of our most valuable partners.

### We should:

- identify community organizations near us
- ask what they need, not just what we need
- find small ways to support each other
- ask our Community Support team for advice if we're unsure who to approach

### Simple question

__Do we have a way to work with community organizations?__

__Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these five questions:

- Do we have a way to work with universities?
- Do we have a way to work with cultural groups?
- Do we have a way to work with businesses?
- Do we have a way to work with NGOs?
- Do we have a way to work with community organizations?

If yes, we have real partnerships that help our house grow.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Ask Community Support for Help
focusAreas.summary: This should be one of the easiest and most visible things to do on our site.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. Instead of figuring out who does what, we just ask one simple question: “What do you need help with?”

We simply choose from options like:

- finance
- venue
- programming
- artist
- marketing
- sponsorship
- operations
- brand

The right category may not always be obvious, and that's fine — Community Support can help direct the request from there.

Our goal is simple:

__Getting help feels as easy as asking one simple question.__

__Step 1. Know What We Need Help With__

Before reaching out, we get clear on what kind of help we actually need.

We don't need to know who does what, just what's going on.

### We should:

- think about what's blocking us or where we're stuck
- pick the category that fits best, like finance, venue, programming, artist, marketing, sponsorship, operations or brand
- not worry about picking the “perfect” category
- ask if we're not sure

### Simple question

__Do we know what we need help with?__

__Step 2. Submit a Simple Support Request__

One simple form lets us ask for help without needing to know who does what.

This should take a minute, not an application process.

### We should:

- use the Simple Support Request Form
- describe what we need in a few sentences
- choose the category that best fits
- submit it whenever we need help, not just in emergencies

### Simple question

__Do we know how to submit a support request?__

__Step 3. Hear Back from Community Support__

Once we ask, Community Support connects us with the right help.

We should expect a real response, not silence.

### We should:

- expect a response within a reasonable time
- follow up if we haven't heard back
- be ready to share more detail if asked
- stay open to different kinds of support, not just what we expected

### Simple question

__Do we know what to expect after we ask?__

__Step 4. Use the Help We Receive__

Getting help is only useful if we actually put it to use.

Asking is the first step, not the last.

### We should:

- apply the advice or support we are given
- ask follow-up questions if something's unclear
- thank whoever helped us
- share what we learned with our team

### Simple question

__Do we make good use of the help we receive?__

__Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we know what we need help with?
- Do we know how to submit a support request?
- Do we know what to expect after we ask?
- Do we make good use of the help we receive?

If yes, asking for help feels simple and easy.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__

focusAreas.title: Learn from Other Palestine Houses
focusAreas.summary: We're part of a network of houses, and we can learn a lot from each other.
focusAreas.guideMd:
This does not need to be complicated. Keep knowledge-sharing simple.

We simply need to:

- share a good idea when we find one that works
- write up a simple success story now and then
- read what other houses are sharing
- borrow ideas that fit our own house

What is worth sharing may differ from house to house, so we should share what feels genuinely useful, not everything.

Our goal is simple:

__A house that learns from and contributes to the wider network.__

__Step 1. Share a Good Idea When It Works__

If something works well for us, sharing it can help another house avoid reinventing it.

Small ideas often help the most.

### We should:

- notice when something we tried works particularly well
- use the Good Idea Sharing Template
- keep it short and specific
- share it even if it feels small

### Simple question

__Do we share good ideas when we find them?__

__Step 2. Write a Simple Success Story Now and Then__

A short success story shows what's possible and can inspire other houses.

This does not need to happen often, just when it matters.

### We should:

- use the Success Story Template
- write it up soon after something goes well
- keep it honest and easy to read
- include a photo if we have one

### Simple question

__Do we write up success stories now and then?__

__Step 3. Read What Other Houses Are Sharing__

Other houses are learning things too, and we can benefit from what they've already figured out.

A few minutes of reading can save us hours of trial and error.

### We should:

- check in on what other houses have shared
- read with an open mind, not just to compare
- note anything that could work for us
- ask questions if something isn't clear

### Simple question

__Do we read what other houses share?__

__Step 4. Borrow Ideas That Fit Our Own House__

A good idea from elsewhere still needs to be adapted to fit our own space, team and community.

Copying exactly rarely works as well as adapting.

### We should:

- try ideas that genuinely fit our house
- adjust them rather than copying exactly
- test on a small scale first
- share back how it went

### Simple question

__Do we adapt good ideas to fit our own house?__

__Our Final Check__

Before we move on, we should be able to answer yes to these four questions:

- Do we share good ideas when we find them?
- Do we write up success stories now and then?
- Do we read what other houses share?
- Do we adapt good ideas to fit our own house?

If yes, we're learning from and contributing to the wider network.

__Keep it simple.
Ask our Community Support team if anything is unclear.
Keep the important documents together.
Ask when you are unsure.__
